definition: The conditions a deliverable has to satisfy before it is accepted, agreed in advance so that the decision to accept it can be checked objectively.
A method in which acceptance criteria are agreed jointly and turned into acceptance tests before delivery starts.

The obligation of one person to answer for how a task or a project turns out; it rests with a single individual and cannot be shared, unlike responsibility for doing the work, which several people may hold.
A task or group of related tasks in a schedule network, occurring within prescribed limits of time, that must be performed in the accomplishment of a project.

A way of developing a product that suits work whose requirements are highly uncertain and unstable and are expected to change as the project goes on; the scope is worked out in short cycles with frequent feedback.
A diagram in which a large set of ideas, such as those produced in a brainstorming session, is sorted into groups of related items so that they can be reviewed and analysed.
The mindset of the Agile Manifesto's values and principles.
The set of methods used to lessen unfair bias in artificial intelligence models, so that the outcomes they produce are fair to the people they affect.

A computer-based system that works out, from the data it is given, how to produce outputs such as content, predictions, decisions or recommendations that serve stated or implied goals and can affect physical or digital environments. Such systems differ in how autonomously they act and how far they keep adapting once deployed.

A technique for weighing the identified options against each other to choose which options or approaches the project will use to carry out its work, for example whether to build a component or buy it.
A technique that estimates the duration, cost or resources of an activity or project from the actual figures of a similar one.
An activity whose effort cannot be split into discrete pieces and is planned in proportion to the discrete work it supports.
Any document or other item a project, program or portfolio produces to help run it and inform its team, stakeholders and management.
The capability of computational systems to perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as decision-making.

A practice for designing and validating a system with plain-language scripts written as tests before it is built.
Comparing products, processes and practices, in place or planned, with those of similar organizations to find good practices, gather improvement ideas and set a performance yardstick.
A gain or asset, financial or not, that an organization and its stakeholders draw from the outcomes a project or program delivers, such as higher revenue, lower costs or better service.
A document explaining the processes by which a program or project creates, maximizes and sustains its benefits.
A document setting out the work, schedule, tools and resources needed to fully achieve the planned benefits over time.
Another name for an impediment: an obstacle that keeps the team from its objectives.
A way of estimating time, cost or resources by adding up estimates for lower-level work breakdown structure components.
An approved estimate covering a project, program or portfolio, or any of its work breakdown structure elements or schedule activities.
The total of every budget set for a body of work, such as a project or control account.
A graphical representation of work left to do versus time over one timebox.

The activities that help deliver solutions which serve business objectives and keep adding value to the organization.
A document assessing the economic viability of a project, program or portfolio component and validating the benefits it is to deliver.
An organization's reason to change, arising from a current problem or opportunity; it justifies starting a program or project.
A specific, measurable target the business aims to reach; it should align with the organization's objectives.
The document or documents listing every requirement of a specific project.
A constraint the business sets on how the organization should operate, enforced through data and/or processes.
The net, quantifiable gain, tangible and/or intangible, that an organization draws from a business undertaking.
What an organization can do, through a function, a process, a service or some other proficiency, to add value or reach its objectives.
An event or condition, existing or certain to occur, that may give rise to risks.
A diagram (also known as a fishbone diagram or Ishikawa diagram) that shows the causes of a specific event, down to its root cause.

The procedures for managing and controlling changes to project deliverables and documents.
Part of the project management plan that sets up the change control board, defines its authority and says how the change control system will work.
A formal proposal to change a document, a deliverable or a baseline.
The numbering scheme that gives each element of the work breakdown structure a unique identifier.
The practice of placing project team members close together to ease communication, strengthen working relationships and raise productivity.
Part of the project, program or portfolio management plan that sets out how and when information will be handled and distributed, and by whom.
A quality of a project or program, or of its environment, that makes it hard to manage because of human and system behavior and ambiguity.
A predefined part of a project, program or portfolio whose work helps meet its strategic objectives.
Part of the project management plan that sets out the procedures for tracking project artifacts and monitoring and controlling changes to them.
The procedures for tracking project artifacts and monitoring and controlling changes to them.
A restraint on carrying out a project, program, portfolio or process.
An event that could affect the project's execution and may be covered by a reserve.
A document that outlines the actions to follow if trigger conditions defined in advance occur, for example, to minimise the impact of a risk after it has occurred.

The practice of frequently integrating every team member's work and validating the whole.
The range of life cycle approaches, often called hybrid life cycles, that blend predictive elements with iterative and incremental agile ones in varying mixes.
A management control point that integrates scope, schedule, budget and actual cost and compares them with earned value to measure performance.
An action planned for the purpose of bringing the project back on track when deviations from the project's baselines have been identified.

Analysis that turns data into actionable information for decision-making.
The date as of which project status is recorded.
A field to extract knowledge and insights from structured and unstructured data.
